claim: Vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) and Sindbis virus (SINV) are completely restricted in their replication after entry into Lepidopteran cells.
source: We found that two RNA viruses with broad host ranges, vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) and Sindbis virus (SINV), are completely restricted in their replication after entry into Lepidopteran cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing restricted replication of VSV and SINV in LD652 cells, including LUC assays, immunoblots, and titer measurements (Figures 1, 9).

claim: Co-infection with vaccinia virus (VACV) overcomes the restriction of VSV and SINV replication in Lepidopteran cells.
source: This restriction is overcome when cells are co-infected with vaccinia virus (VACV), a vertebrate DNA virus.
evidence: Experimental data show that VACV co-infection dramatically increases VSV and SINV gene expression, protein levels, and viral titers in LD652 cells (Figure 1C-H).

claim: Lepidopteran RNAi pathways restrict RNA virus infection in LD652 cells.
source: Using RNAi screening, we show that Lepidopteran RNAi, Nuclear Factor-κB, and ubiquitin-proteasome pathways restrict RNA virus infection.
evidence: RNAi knockdown of AGO2 and Dicer-2 increased LUC expression ~10-fold in both VSV-LUC and SINV-LUC infected cells (Figure 2C,D).

claim: Nuclear Factor-κB pathways restrict RNA virus infection in LD652 cells.
source: Using RNAi screening, we show that Lepidopteran RNAi, Nuclear Factor-κB, and ubiquitin-proteasome pathways restrict RNA virus infection.
evidence: RNAi knockdown of the NF-κB homolog Relish increased LUC expression ~10-fold in both VSV-LUC and SINV-LUC infected cells (Figure 2C,D).

claim: Ubiquitin-proteasome pathways restrict RNA virus infection in LD652 cells.
source: Using RNAi screening, we show that Lepidopteran RNAi, Nuclear Factor-κB, and ubiquitin-proteasome pathways restrict RNA virus infection.
evidence: RNAi knockdown of ubiquitin-encoding genes increased LUC expression nearly 1000-fold in VSV-LUC-infected cells and 10-fold in SINV-LUC-infected cells (Figure 2C,D).

claim: VACV protein A51R can partially overcome virus restriction in Lepidopteran cells.
source: Surprisingly, a highly conserved, uncharacterized VACV protein, A51R, can partially overcome this virus restriction.
evidence: RNAi knockdown of A51R reduced VSV rescue by VACV-WR (Figure 4B), and deletion of A51R resulted in 100-fold reduction in VSV gene expression (Figure 4C). Transient expression of Flag-A51R alone increased VSV gene expression ~60-fold (Figure 4E).

claim: A51R is critical for VACV replication in vertebrate cells.
source: We show that A51R is also critical for VACV replication in vertebrate cells and for pathogenesis in mice.
evidence: Growth curve analyses showed that ΔA51R strain exhibited reduced replication compared to VACV-WR in BSC-40 cells at high MOI (Figure 10B).

claim: A51R is critical for VACV pathogenesis in mice.
source: We show that A51R is also critical for VACV replication in vertebrate cells and for pathogenesis in mice.
evidence: Mice infected with ΔA51R showed significantly improved survival (4/5 survived) compared to VACV-WR infected mice (0/5 survived) (Figure 10D). ΔA51R-infected mice had significantly lower virus titers in ovaries at day 6 post-infection (Figure 10F).

claim: A51R colocalizes with host microtubules.
source: Interestingly, A51R colocalizes with, and stabilizes, host microtubules and also associates with ubiquitin.
evidence: Confocal microscopy showed that Flag-A51R staining significantly overlapped with cellular tubulin staining (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: A51R stabilizes host microtubules.
source: Interestingly, A51R colocalizes with, and stabilizes, host microtubules and also associates with ubiquitin.
evidence: In the presence of nocodazole, filamentous drug-resistant MT structures were abundant in ΔA51RFA51R-infected BSC-40 cells but absent in mock-infected and ΔA51R-infected cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C). Similar results were observed with vincristine treatment (Figure 7B).

claim: A51R associates with ubiquitin.
source: Interestingly, A51R colocalizes with, and stabilizes, host microtubules and also associates with ubiquitin.
evidence: MuDPIT mass spectrometry analysis identified ubiquitin as one of the four most-enriched proteins in Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates from LD652 cells (Table 2).

claim: A51R promotes viral protein stability.
source: We show that A51R promotes viral protein stability, possibly by preventing ubiquitin-dependent targeting of viral proteins for destruction.
evidence: Radiolabeling and chase experiments showed that VSV N protein had a half-life of ~2 hours in ΔA51R co-infections compared to >8 hours in VACV-WR co-infections (Figure 9B,C).

claim: A51R does not affect viral mRNA translation rates.
source: Using radiolabeling and immunoblotting, we show that A51R does not affect viral mRNA translation rates but does promote virus protein stability
evidence: Pulse-labeling experiments showed similar levels of nascent VSV N protein synthesis in both VACV-WR and ΔA51R co-infections (Figure 9A), indicating that A51R does not affect translation rates.

claim: VSV and SINV restriction in LD652 cells occurs post-entry.
source: The low level, but above background, LUC activity detected in VSV-LUC and SINV-LUC singly-infected LD652 cultures suggested that these viruses are blocked at one or more steps post-entry.
evidence: VSV and SINV capsids were detected inside singly-infected LD652 cells by confocal microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), and viral transcripts were detected at 8 hpi by RT-PCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).

claim: Host transcription is required for RNA virus restriction in LD652 cells.
source: To ask if host transcription was required to resist RNA virus infection, we treated VSV-LUC and SINV-LUC-infected LD652 cells with increasing doses of actinomycin D (ActD)
evidence: Treatment with ActD, which blocks host transcription, increased VSV and SINV gene expression in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2B), suggesting that host transcription is required for the antiviral response.

claim: VACV early gene expression is required for RNA virus rescue in LD652 cells.
source: To test if VACV binding and entry into LD652 cells is sufficient to rescue RNA virus infection in the absence of VACV gene expression, we co-infected LD652 cells with VSV or SINV and a heat-inactivated strain of VACV
evidence: Heat-inactivated VACV failed to rescue VSV or SINV replication (Figure 3A), and AraC treatment (which blocks VACV DNA replication and late gene expression) did not prevent rescue (Figure 3B), indicating that early VACV gene expression is required.

claim: VACV-MVA is defective in rescuing RNA virus replication compared to VACV-WR.
source: We found that the attenuated modified VACV strain Ankara (VACV-MVA) failed to fully rescue either VSV or SINV as compared to either VACV-WR or Copenhagen strains
evidence: LUC assays and immunoblots showed that VACV-MVA produced significantly lower levels of VSV and SINV gene expression compared to VACV-WR or Copenhagen strains (Figure 3C,D,E).

claim: A51R is expressed as an early VACV protein.
source: immunoblot of lysates from a time course of A51RFA51R infection confirmed that Flag-A51R is expressed early in VACV infection, as it was detected by 2 hpi in the absence or presence of AraC
evidence: Immunoblot analysis showed Flag-A51R protein was detected at 2 hpi in both the presence and absence of AraC (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).

claim: A51R expression is sufficient to rescue VSV and SINV infection in LD652 cells in the absence of other VACV components.
source: These results indicate that Flag-A51R expression is sufficient to overcome the host restriction to RNA virus replication in the absence of other VACV proteins.
evidence: Transient transfection of Flag-A51R alone (without VACV infection) resulted in ~60-fold increase in VSV and 12-fold increase in SINV gene expression (Figure 4E), and increased viral titers (Figure 4G,H).

claim: A51R-mediated VSV replication reduces LD652 cell viability.
source: This reduced cell viability was not observed when Flag-GFP-transfected cells were infected with VSV-LUC, suggesting that active viral replication was required to induce cell death
evidence: Trypan blue exclusion assays showed that cell viability dropped to ~50% by day 7 in Flag-A51R-transfected, VSV-infected cells, but not in Flag-GFP-transfected, VSV-infected cells (Figure 4I).

claim: A51R proteins from multiple poxviruses can rescue RNA virus replication in LD652 cells.
source: We found that A51R homologs from cowpox virus (CPXV), ectromelia virus (ECTV), deerpox virus (DPXV), and Yaba-like disease virus (YLDV) all rescued VSV replication to levels similar to VACV A51R
evidence: LUC assays showed that A51R homologs from CPXV, ECTV, DPXV, and YLDV all increased VSV gene expression to similar levels as VACV A51R, while MYXV A51R showed reduced rescue ability (Figure 5).

claim: A51R promotes RNA virus infection in multiple Lepidopteran cell lines.
source: We found that VACV-WR co-infection or Flag-A51R expression also rescued VSV replication in L. dispar-derived embryonic (LdEP) cells, Spodoptera frugiperda-derived Sf9 cells, and Manduca sexta-derived GV-1 cells
evidence: LUC assays and viral titer measurements showed that A51R or VACV-WR rescued VSV replication in LdEP, Sf9, and GV-1 cells (Figure 6A-E).

claim: A51R does not enhance VSV replication in Drosophila melanogaster-derived DL1 cells.
source: In contrast, A51R expression did not enhance VSV replication in D. melanogaster-derived DL1 cells
evidence: LUC assays showed no significant increase in VSV gene expression in DL1 cells transfected with Flag-A51R compared to Flag-GFP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and VACV-WR co-infection also did not enhance VSV replication (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).

claim: A51R protects microtubules from depolymerization by nocodazole.
source: In the presence of nocodazole, MT structures were essentially absent in mock-infected and ΔA51R-infected cells. However filamentous, drug-resistant 'MT pieces' were abundant in ΔA51RFA51R-infected BSC-40 cells
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy showed that nocodazole-resistant MT structures were present in ΔA51RFA51R-infected cells but absent in mock-infected and ΔA51R-infected cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).

claim: VACV-MVA A51R protein is deficient in forming filament-like structures and protecting MTs from depolymerization.
source: We therefore examined Flag-MVAA51R protein localization in nocodazole-treated cells and found that, although Flag-MVAA51R staining stained small punctate structures throughout the cytoplasm that overlapped with tubulin, large drug-resistant MT-like structures failed to form
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy showed that Flag-MVAA51R formed only small punctate structures and did not form large drug-resistant MT structures in nocodazole-treated cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).

claim: A51R localization to and stabilization of MTs does not require other VACV proteins.
source: To ask if Flag-A51R localization to and stabilization of MTs requires other VACV proteins, we transfected BSC-40 cells with a plasmid expressing Flag-A51R. We found that Flag-A51R expression was sufficient for both localization to, and stabilization of, MTs
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy of transfected (not infected) cells showed that Flag-A51R colocalized with tubulin and formed nocodazole-resistant structures in the absence of VACV infection (Figure 7A).

claim: A51R stabilizes MTs in Lepidopteran cells.
source: Similar results were obtained in LD652 cells treated with the MT-depolymerizing drug vincristine
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy showed that Flag-A51R formed filamentous structures that colocalized with tubulin in vincristine-treated LD652 cells (Figure 7B).

claim: MT stabilization by A51R is insufficient for full RNA virus rescue.
source: Based on the conservation of RNA virus rescue and MT stabilization functions of poxvirus A51R proteins, we wondered if these two functions could be separated.
evidence: The A51RR321A mutant retained the ability to form filamentous structures and stabilize MTs (Figure 8D) but showed significantly reduced VSV rescue ability compared to wild-type A51R (Figure 8B), indicating that MT stabilization alone is insufficient for full rescue.

claim: A51R co-immunoprecipitates with myosin II essential light chain, ubiquitin, and ribosomal protein S15.
source: Filtering differential normalized spectral abundance factor (NSAF) values from both control and Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates identified the four most-enriched proteins in Flag-A51R treatments. These proteins are the target Flag-A51R, myosin II essential light chain (a constituent of the actomyosin cytoskeleton), Ub, and ribosomal protein S15
evidence: MuDPIT mass spectrometry analysis of Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates from LD652 cells identified myosin II essential light chain, ubiquitin, and ribosomal protein S15 as enriched proteins (Table 2).

claim: A51R does not affect VSV mRNA translation rates.
source: Pulse-labeling experiments showed similar levels of nascent VSV N protein synthesis in both VACV-WR and ΔA51R co-infections
evidence: Radiolabeling experiments with [35S]methionine showed similar amounts of newly synthesized VSV N protein in VACV-WR and ΔA51R co-infections after a 2-hour pulse (Figure 9A).

claim: A51R increases VSV protein stability.
source: VSV N protein had a half-life of ~2 hours in ΔA51R co-infections compared to >8 hours in VACV-WR co-infections
evidence: Pulse-chase experiments showed that radiolabeled VSV N protein degraded much more rapidly in ΔA51R co-infections (half-life ~2 hours) compared to VACV-WR co-infections (half-life >8 hours) (Figure 9B,C).

claim: ΔA51R VACV strain exhibits reduced replication at high MOI in vertebrate cells.
source: At a low MOI of 0.03, the ΔA51R, VACV-WR, and ΔA51RFA51R strains replicated to similar titers by 24 hpi. However, at a high MOI of 3, the ΔA51R strain exhibited ∼10-fold lower titers than VACV-WR or ΔA51RFA51R strains by 24 hpi
evidence: Growth curve analyses in BSC-40 cells showed that ΔA51R had similar titers to VACV-WR at low MOI (Figure 10A) but ~10-fold lower titers at high MOI (Figure 10B).

claim: ΔA51R VACV strain is attenuated for virulence in mice.
source: Both VACV-WR and ΔA51R infections led to rapid weight loss of animals by days 4 and 5, respectively. In animals infected with VACV-WR, weight loss continued on days 6–7 post-infection, with 5/5 animals ultimately succumbing to infection by day 7. In contrast, only 1/5 animals infected with the ΔA51R strain died by day 7, while the remaining animals recovered from infection, gained weight and survived until the end of the 28 day experiment
evidence: Mouse infection experiments showed that 5/5 VACV-WR-infected mice died by day 7, while only 1/5 ΔA51R-infected mice died, with the remaining 4/5 surviving to day 28 (Figure 10C,D).

claim: ΔA51R VACV strain shows reduced viral spread to distant tissues in mice.
source: By day 6 post-infection, however, we detected significantly higher virus titers (p<0.05) in the ovaries of all VACV-WR-infected animals compared to ΔA51R-infected animals, in which virus was detectable in only 1/5 animals
evidence: Viral titer measurements showed significantly higher titers in ovaries of VACV-WR-infected mice compared to ΔA51R-infected mice at day 6 post-infection (Figure 10F).

claim: The reduced replication of ΔA51R is not due to reduced EEV production.
source: The reduced replication of the ΔA51R strain at later time points of infection during in vitro and in vivo infections was not caused by a reduction in the extracellular enveloped (EEV) form of VACV
evidence: Analysis showed that ΔA51R cultures shed ~twofold higher levels of EEV than VACV-WR cultures, despite having ~10-fold lower total virus titers (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Loss of A51R does not make VACV more susceptible to interferon.
source: ΔA51R titers, however, were similarly reduced at this time point, suggesting that loss of A51R does not make VACV more susceptible to the antiviral effects of IFN
evidence: IFN pre-treatment reduced both VACV-WR and ΔA51R titers by ~10-fold, indicating similar susceptibility to IFN (Figure 10—figure supplement 1D).

claim: VACV can undergo early gene expression, DNA replication, and late gene expression in LD652 cells, but the infection is abortive.
source: During infection of LD652 cells, VACV undergoes early gene expression, DNA replication and late gene expression, but the infection is abortive due to a defect in one or more steps of virion morphogenesis
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Li et al., 1998.

claim: VACV entry and early gene expression occur in Drosophila cells, but viral DNA replication and late gene expression are blocked.
source: VACV entry and early gene expression have also been documented in Drosophila cells, however viral DNA replication and subsequent late gene expression were not detected, indicating that VACV replication is blocked earlier in its life cycle in Drosophila cells than in LD652 cells
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Moser et al., 2010.

claim: RNAi screening of VACV-infected Drosophila cells has identified multiple host factors required for VACV entry.
source: Despite these limitations, RNAi screening of VACV-infected Drosophila cells has identified multiple host factors required for VACV entry in eukaryotic hosts
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Moser et al., 2010.

claim: VSV and SINV replicate in a wide range of invertebrate and vertebrate hosts.
source: Here we explore RNA virus-Lepidopteran host interactions by infecting LD652 cells with the (−)-sense ssRNA vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) or the (+)-sense ssRNA Sindbis virus (SINV), both of which replicate in a wide range of invertebrate and vertebrate hosts
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Letchworth et al., 1999; Xiong et al., 1989).

claim: Antiviral RNAi pathways are deeply conserved in vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: A role for AGO2 and Dicer-2 in Lepidopteran restriction to RNA virus replication is consistent with the deep conservation of RNAi-based antiviral immunity in vertebrates and invertebrates
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Kingsolver et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013; Maillard et al., 2013) and draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: The IMD pathway plays an antiviral role in Diptera.
source: Our findings are consistent with recent reports that the IMD pathway plays an antiviral role in Diptera
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Avadhanula et al., 2009; Costa et al., 2009).

claim: Several natural viral pathogens of Lepidoptera encode ubiquitin-like molecules.
source: Interestingly, several natural viral pathogens of Lepidoptera encode Ub-like molecules, suggesting that Ub may be required for their life cycle
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Barry et al., 2010.

claim: Baculovirus-encoded ubiquitin homologs can inhibit ubiquitin chain elongation.
source: For example, baculovirus-encoded Ub homologs can inhibit Ub chain elongation
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Haas et al., 1996.

claim: Several viruses encode potent deubiquitinating enzymes.
source: and several viruses encode potent deubiquitinating enzymes
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Lindner, 2007.

claim: VACV enhances VSV replication in mammalian cell culture through IFN response antagonists E3L and B18R.
source: In mammalian cell culture, VACV also enhances VSV replication, but the VACV-encoded IFN response antagonists E3L and B18R are the major determinants of this rescue
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Le Boeuf et al., 2010; Shors et al., 1998).

claim: The interferon response appears to be vertebrate-specific.
source: Since the IFN response appears to be vertebrate-specific
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Mukherjee et al., 2014 and draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Microtubules have been implicated in promoting VSV and SINV gene expression.
source: Previous studies implicate MTs in promoting VSV and SINV gene expression
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Qiu et al., 1998; Heinrich et al., 2010).

claim: Tubulin has been shown to promote VSV RNA polymerase activity in vitro.
source: and tubulin has been shown to promote VSV RNA polymerase activity in vitro
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Moyer et al., 1986.

claim: VSV transport to the cell surface is reported to be microtubule-dependent.
source: Furthermore, VSV transport to the cell surface is reported to be MT-dependent
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Das et al., 2006.

claim: A recent study found no effect of microtubule depolymerization on VSV and SINV replication.
source: However, a recent study found no effect of MT depolymerization on VSV and SINV replication
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Matthews et al., 2013.

claim: VACV-WR infection causes redistribution of endosomes to large perinuclear clusters.
source: Previously it has been shown that VACV-WR infection causes redistribution of endosomes from dispersed cytosolic locations to large perinuclear clusters, suggesting that outward, MT-dependent endosomal trafficking might be impaired during VACV infection
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Schepis et al., 2006.

claim: Endosome clustering during VACV infection requires early gene expression and activities lacking in VACV-MVA.
source: This endosome clustering phenomenon requires early gene expression and one or more activities lacking in VACV-MVA
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Schepis et al., 2006.

claim: VSV can utilize endocytic modes of entry.
source: It is possible that these punctate structures represent virions trapped inside endosomes as both VSV (Mire et al., 2010) and SINV (DeTulleo and Kirchhausen, 1998) can utilize endocytic modes of entry.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Mire et al., 2010.

claim: SINV can utilize endocytic modes of entry.
source: It is possible that these punctate structures represent virions trapped inside endosomes as both VSV (Mire et al., 2010) and SINV (DeTulleo and Kirchhausen, 1998) can utilize endocytic modes of entry.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by DeTulleo and Kirchhausen, 1998.

claim: VACV-MVA releases 2-3 times more EEV particles than VACV-WR.
source: Alteration of MT-dependent trafficking by A51R may help explain why both VACV-MVA (Meiser et al., 2003) and ΔA51R (this study) strains release 2-3-times more EEV particles than does VACV-WR.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Meiser et al., 2003 for VACV-MVA, and by data in this study for ΔA51R (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).

claim: EEV release is microtubule-dependent.
source: The release of EEV is MT-dependent
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Ploubidou et al., 2000.

claim: EEV is known to elicit neutralizing antibodies.
source: and EEV is known to elicit neutralizing antibodies
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Smith et al., 2002 and draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: The Dryvax strain of VACV encodes a fragmented A51R gene.
source: Interestingly, the Dryvax strain of VACV, which is used for smallpox vaccination, encodes a fragmented A51R gene
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Qin et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of A51R function may contribute to the induction of poxvirus immunity.
source: These observations, along with the attenuated virulence of ΔA51R strain in vivo, raise the intriguing possibility that loss of A51R function contributes to the induction of poxvirus immunity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that Dryvax (a vaccine strain) has a fragmented A51R gene and that ΔA51R is attenuated in mice.

claim: Nocodazole-resistant MT structures were previously observed in VACV-infected cells but not in VACV-MVA-infected cells.
source: Thus, the presence or absence of functional A51R could explain why the nocodazole-resistant 'MT pieces' previously observed in VACV-infected cells were not observed in uninfected or VACV-MVA-infected cells
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Ploubidou et al., 2000; Schepis et al., 2006).

claim: A51R may overcome host restriction by preventing ubiquitin-dependent targeting of viral proteins for degradation.
source: We show that A51R promotes viral protein stability, possibly by preventing ubiquitin-dependent targeting of viral proteins for destruction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations that A51R associates with ubiquitin, promotes viral protein stability, and that UPS inhibition enhances viral replication.

claim: Lepidopteran cells may have a mechanism to target protein synthesis coupled to cytoplasmic transcription.
source: This latter hypothesis predicts that Lepidopterans cells might have a mechanism to target protein synthesis that is coupled to cytoplasmic transcription.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observation that UPS inhibition only enhanced viral (cytoplasmic) but not plasmid-based (nuclear) LUC expression.

claim: A51R may subvert host antiviral responses by perturbing MT-dependent transport of host factors and/or organelles.
source: It is possible that A51R subverts host antiviral responses partly by perturbing MT-dependent transport of host factors and/or organelles.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on A51R's MT-stabilizing properties and previous observations of endosome clustering during VACV infection.

claim: A51R may induce endosome clustering to overcome a host mechanism that traps viruses in endosomes.
source: A51R fits these criteria, and thus could be the VACV factor that induces endosome clustering, perhaps to overcome a host mechanism that could otherwise trap viruses in endosomes.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on A51R's properties and previous observations of endosome clustering during VACV infection.

claim: A51R may attenuate virion transport along MTs to reduce EEV release and escape immune activation.
source: Thus it is possible that A51R attenuates virion transport along MTs, and subsequent EEV release, in order to allow the virus to escape activation of host immune responses
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that ΔA51R releases more EEV and that EEV elicits neutralizing antibodies.

claim: A51R-dependent sequestration of ubiquitin may overcome a ubiquitin-dependent antiviral mechanism.
source: Although we do not yet know specifically how A51R promotes virus protein stability, it is possible that A51R-dependent sequestration of Ub (or removal of Ub from viral proteins) acts to overcome a Ub-dependent mechanism that either activates host antiviral protein effectors or directly targets nascent viral proteins for destruction.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on A51R's association with ubiquitin and its effect on viral protein stability.

claim: VACV can rescue VSV and SINV replication as late as 24 hours post-RNA virus infection.
source: Remarkably, we could also rescue VSV and SINV gene expression (albeit to reduced levels) by the addition of VACV-WR as late as 24 hpi with RNA virus
evidence: Experimental data showed that VACV-WR added at 24 hpi still increased VSV and SINV gene expression, though to reduced levels compared to immediate co-infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).

claim: Actinomycin D treatment increases VSV and SINV gene expression in LD652 cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: we treated VSV-LUC and SINV-LUC-infected LD652 cells with increasing doses of actinomycin D (ActD)
evidence: LUC assays showed that ActD treatment increased VSV and SINV gene expression in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2B).

claim: RNAi knockdown of Effete increases VSV and SINV gene expression approximately 10-fold.
source: Knockdowns of four transcripts, encoding homologs of the RNAi pathway proteins AGO2 and Dicer-2, the Nuclear Factor kappa B (NF-κB)-homolog Relish, and the E2 ubiquitin (Ub)-conjugating enzyme Effete, increased LUC expression ∼10-fold in both VSV-LUC- and SINV-LUC-infected cells.
evidence: RNAi experiments showed that knockdown of Effete increased LUC expression ~10-fold in both VSV-LUC and SINV-LUC infected cells (Figure 2C,D).

claim: Treatment with the E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme inhibitor PYR-41 enhances viral but not plasmid-driven LUC expression.
source: We found that viral-driven, but not plasmid-driven (p166-LUC), LUC expression was enhanced in experiments aimed at inhibiting the UPS, including: (i) exposure to Ub RNAi, (ii) treatment with inhibitors of either E1 Ub-activating enzymes (PYR-41)
evidence: Experimental data showed that PYR-41 treatment increased viral-driven LUC expression but not plasmid-driven LUC expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 enhances viral but not plasmid-driven LUC expression.
source: We found that viral-driven, but not plasmid-driven (p166-LUC), LUC expression was enhanced in experiments aimed at inhibiting the UPS, including: (i) exposure to Ub RNAi, (ii) treatment with inhibitors of either E1 Ub-activating enzymes (PYR-41), or the proteasome (MG132)
evidence: Experimental data showed that MG132 treatment increased viral-driven LUC expression but not plasmid-driven LUC expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Expression of wild-type coronavirus PLpro deubiquitinase, but not a catalytically inactive mutant, enhances viral but not plasmid-driven LUC expression.
source: We found that viral-driven, but not plasmid-driven (p166-LUC), LUC expression was enhanced in experiments aimed at inhibiting the UPS, including: ... (iii) transient expression of a wild-type (but not a catalytically inactive) coronavirus-encoded deubiquitinase (PLpro)
evidence: Experimental data showed that wild-type PLpro, but not the catalytic mutant PLproC112A, increased viral-driven LUC expression but not plasmid-driven LUC expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Heat inactivation of VACV prevents rescue of VSV and SINV replication.
source: To test if VACV binding and entry into LD652 cells is sufficient to rescue RNA virus infection in the absence of VACV gene expression, we co-infected LD652 cells with VSV or SINV and a heat-inactivated strain of VACV
evidence: Experimental data showed that heat-inactivated VACV failed to rescue VSV or SINV replication (Figure 3A).

claim: AraC treatment does not prevent VACV-mediated rescue of VSV and SINV replication.
source: To determine if VACV DNA replication and late gene expression were required for RNA virus rescue, we treated co-infected cells with cytosine arabinoside (AraC), which blocks VACV DNA replication. We found that AraC treatment did not prevent VACV-mediated rescue of VSV or SINV replication
evidence: Experimental data showed that AraC treatment did not prevent VACV-mediated rescue of VSV or SINV (Figure 3B).

claim: VACV Copenhagen strain rescues VSV and SINV replication similarly to VACV-WR.
source: We found that the attenuated modified VACV strain Ankara (VACV-MVA) failed to fully rescue either VSV or SINV as compared to either VACV-WR or Copenhagen strains
evidence: LUC assays showed that VACV Copenhagen rescued VSV and SINV to similar levels as VACV-WR (Figure 3C,D).

claim: RNAi knockdown of A51R reduces VACV-mediated rescue of VSV replication.
source: We found that RNAi knockdown of A51R transcripts reduced VSV rescue by VACV-WR by ∼10-fold
evidence: RNAi experiments showed that A51R knockdown reduced VSV rescue by ~10-fold (Figure 4B).

claim: Deletion of A51R results in 100-fold reduction in VSV gene expression during VACV co-infection.
source: Importantly, we found that co-infection with ΔA51R resulted in a 100-fold reduction in VSV gene expression relative to co-infection with VACV-WR
evidence: LUC assays showed that ΔA51R co-infection resulted in 100-fold reduction in VSV gene expression compared to VACV-WR (Figure 4C).

claim: Revertant VACV strains expressing Flag-A51R restore VSV rescue ability.
source: VSV was rescued by co-infecting with revertant VACV strains, expressing a Flag-tagged A51R gene (Flag-A51R) reintroduced into either the A51R locus (ΔA51RFA51R) or the VACV thymidine kinase (J2R) locus (ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFA51R).
evidence: LUC assays showed that revertant strains ΔA51RFA51R and ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFA51R restored VSV rescue to levels similar to VACV-WR (Figure 4C).

claim: VACV-MVA A51R protein fails to fully rescue VSV replication.
source: Furthermore, consistent with the idea that the VACV-MVA A51R protein is not functional, we found that the ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFMVAA51R strain failed to fully rescue VSV
evidence: LUC assays showed that the ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFMVAA51R strain failed to fully rescue VSV compared to strains expressing wild-type A51R (Figure 4C).

claim: A51R is required for full rescue of SINV replication by VACV, but other VACV factors also contribute.
source: A51R was also required for full rescue of SINV replication by VACV. However, we noticed that ΔA51R and ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFMVAA51R strains exhibited only a moderate fourfold reduction in their ability to promote SINV gene expression as compared to 100-fold reductions for VSV. These findings suggest that other VACV factors in addition to A51R promote SINV replication in LD652 cells.
evidence: LUC assays showed that ΔA51R had only a 4-fold reduction in SINV rescue compared to 100-fold reduction for VSV, suggesting additional VACV factors contribute to SINV rescue (Figure 4C,D).

claim: Transient expression of Flag-A51R increases VSV gene expression approximately 60-fold.
source: Although only ∼40–60% of cells expressed detectable Flag-A51R protein (data not shown), we observed an ∼60-fold increase in VSV and 12-fold increase in SINV gene expression relative to control transfections with empty p166 vector or vector encoding Flag-tagged GFP (Flag-GFP)
evidence: LUC assays showed that Flag-A51R transfection increased VSV gene expression ~60-fold compared to controls (Figure 4E).

claim: Transient expression of Flag-A51R increases SINV gene expression approximately 12-fold.
source: Although only ∼40–60% of cells expressed detectable Flag-A51R protein (data not shown), we observed an ∼60-fold increase in VSV and 12-fold increase in SINV gene expression relative to control transfections with empty p166 vector or vector encoding Flag-tagged GFP (Flag-GFP)
evidence: LUC assays showed that Flag-A51R transfection increased SINV gene expression ~12-fold compared to controls (Figure 4E).

claim: A51R homologs from CPXV, ECTV, DPXV, and YLDV rescue VSV replication to levels similar to VACV A51R.
source: We found that A51R homologs from cowpox virus (CPXV), ectromelia virus (ECTV), deerpox virus (DPXV), and Yaba-like disease virus (YLDV) all rescued VSV replication to levels similar to VACV A51R
evidence: LUC assays showed that A51R homologs from CPXV, ECTV, DPXV, and YLDV increased VSV gene expression to similar levels as VACV A51R (Figure 5).

claim: Myxoma virus A51R homolog shows reduced VSV rescue ability compared to other poxvirus A51R proteins.
source: In contrast, the myxoma virus (MYXV) A51R homolog showed reduced rescue ability
evidence: LUC assays showed that MYXV A51R had reduced VSV rescue ability compared to other poxvirus A51R proteins (Figure 5).

claim: VACV-WR co-infection rescues VSV replication in L. dispar-derived embryonic (LdEP) cells.
source: We found that VACV-WR co-infection or Flag-A51R expression also rescued VSV replication in L. dispar-derived embryonic (LdEP) cells
evidence: LUC assays showed that VACV-WR co-infection increased VSV gene expression in LdEP cells (Figure 6A).

claim: Flag-A51R expression rescues VSV replication in Spodoptera frugiperda-derived Sf9 cells.
source: We found that VACV-WR co-infection or Flag-A51R expression also rescued VSV replication in ... Spodoptera frugiperda-derived Sf9 cells
evidence: LUC assays and viral titer measurements showed that Flag-A51R expression increased VSV gene expression and titers in Sf9 cells (Figure 6B,C).

claim: Flag-A51R expression rescues VSV replication in Manduca sexta-derived GV-1 cells.
source: We found that VACV-WR co-infection or Flag-A51R expression also rescued VSV replication in ... Manduca sexta-derived GV-1 cells
evidence: LUC assays and viral titer measurements showed that Flag-A51R expression increased VSV gene expression and titers in GV-1 cells (Figure 6D,E).

claim: Flag-A51R forms aggregate-like and filamentous structures in the cytoplasm of BSC-40 cells.
source: We found that Flag-A51R, expressed under its natural promoter from the ΔA51RFA51R virus, formed both aggregate-like as well as filamentous structures in the cytoplasm of African green monkey-derived (BSC-40) cells.
evidence: Confocal microscopy showed that Flag-A51R formed aggregate-like and filamentous structures in BSC-40 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Flag-A51R staining significantly overlaps with cellular tubulin staining.
source: This staining pattern significantly overlapped with that of cellular tubulin, suggesting that A51R associates with a subset of MTs
evidence: Confocal microscopy showed significant overlap between Flag-A51R and tubulin staining (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: Deconvolution of confocal images reveals Flag-A51R staining localized on intact microtubule tracks.
source: Indeed deconvolution of images from these experiments revealed Flag-A51R staining localized on intact MT tracks
evidence: Deconvolved confocal microscopy images showed Flag-A51R staining on intact MT tracks (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The A51RR321A mutant shows significantly reduced VSV rescue ability compared to wild-type A51R.
source: alanine substitution of residue R321, which lies within the C-terminal region of A51R that is missing in VACV-MVA A51R, yielded a mutant protein (A51RR321A) that was expressed at levels similar to wild-type A51R but displayed significantly reduced VSV rescue ability
evidence: LUC assays showed that A51RR321A had significantly reduced VSV rescue ability compared to wild-type A51R (Figure 8B), despite similar protein expression levels (Figure 8C).

claim: The A51RR321A mutant retains the ability to form filamentous structures and stabilize microtubules.
source: Importantly, the A51RR321A mutant retained the ability to form filamentous structures and stabilize MTs
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy showed that A51RR321A formed filamentous structures that colocalized with tubulin in vincristine-treated cells, similar to wild-type A51R (Figure 8D).

claim: Myosin II essential light chain is enriched in Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates from LD652 cells.
source: Filtering differential normalized spectral abundance factor (NSAF) values from both control and Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates identified the four most-enriched proteins in Flag-A51R treatments. These proteins are the target Flag-A51R, myosin II essential light chain (a constituent of the actomyosin cytoskeleton), Ub, and ribosomal protein S15
evidence: MuDPIT mass spectrometry analysis identified myosin II essential light chain as one of the most-enriched proteins in Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates (Table 2).

claim: Ribosomal protein S15 is enriched in Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates from LD652 cells.
source: Filtering differential normalized spectral abundance factor (NSAF) values from both control and Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates identified the four most-enriched proteins in Flag-A51R treatments. These proteins are the target Flag-A51R, myosin II essential light chain (a constituent of the actomyosin cytoskeleton), Ub, and ribosomal protein S15
evidence: MuDPIT mass spectrometry analysis identified ribosomal protein S15 as one of the most-enriched proteins in Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates (Table 2).

claim: Similar levels of nascent VSV N protein are synthesized during VACV-WR and ΔA51R co-infections.
source: Pulse-labeling experiments showed similar levels of nascent VSV N protein synthesis in both VACV-WR and ΔA51R co-infections
evidence: Radiolabeling experiments showed similar amounts of newly synthesized VSV N protein in VACV-WR and ΔA51R co-infections after a 2-hour pulse (Figure 9A).

claim: VSV N protein has a half-life of approximately 2 hours in ΔA51R co-infections.
source: VSV N protein had a half-life of ~2 hours in ΔA51R co-infections compared to >8 hours in VACV-WR co-infections
evidence: Pulse-chase experiments showed that radiolabeled VSV N protein had a half-life of ~2 hours in ΔA51R co-infections (Figure 9B,C).

claim: VSV N protein has a half-life of greater than 8 hours in VACV-WR co-infections.
source: VSV N protein had a half-life of ~2 hours in ΔA51R co-infections compared to >8 hours in VACV-WR co-infections
evidence: Pulse-chase experiments showed that radiolabeled VSV N protein had a half-life of >8 hours in VACV-WR co-infections (Figure 9B,C).

claim: At low MOI, ΔA51R, VACV-WR, and ΔA51RFA51R strains replicate to similar titers by 24 hours post-infection in BSC-40 cells.
source: At a low MOI of 0.03, the ΔA51R, VACV-WR, and ΔA51RFA51R strains replicated to similar titers by 24 hpi.
evidence: Growth curve analyses showed similar titers for all three strains at low MOI by 24 hpi (Figure 10A).

claim: At high MOI, ΔA51R strain exhibits approximately 10-fold lower titers than VACV-WR or ΔA51RFA51R strains by 24 hours post-infection in BSC-40 cells.
source: However, at a high MOI of 3, the ΔA51R strain exhibited ∼10-fold lower titers than VACV-WR or ΔA51RFA51R strains by 24 hpi
evidence: Growth curve analyses showed that ΔA51R had ~10-fold lower titers than VACV-WR or ΔA51RFA51R at high MOI by 24 hpi (Figure 10B).

claim: 5 out of 5 VACV-WR-infected mice died by day 7 post-infection.
source: In animals infected with VACV-WR, weight loss continued on days 6–7 post-infection, with 5/5 animals ultimately succumbing to infection by day 7.
evidence: Survival data showed that all 5 VACV-WR-infected mice died by day 7 (Figure 10D).

claim: Only 1 out of 5 ΔA51R-infected mice died by day 7 post-infection, with the remaining 4 surviving to day 28.
source: In contrast, only 1/5 animals infected with the ΔA51R strain died by day 7, while the remaining animals recovered from infection, gained weight and survived until the end of the 28 day experiment
evidence: Survival data showed that only 1/5 ΔA51R-infected mice died by day 7, with 4/5 surviving to day 28 (Figure 10D).

claim: VACV-WR and ΔA51R replicate to similar titers in lung tissue by day 4 post-infection.
source: After four days of infection, both VACV-WR and ΔA51R viruses replicated to similar titers in lung tissue, the primary site of infection.
evidence: Viral titer measurements showed similar titers in lungs for both strains at day 4 post-infection (Figure 10E).

claim: By day 6 post-infection, there is a trend toward lower ΔA51R titers in the lungs, although not statistically significant.
source: By day 6, however, a trend toward lower ΔA51R titers in the lungs was observed, although this difference was not statistically significant (p=0.05)
evidence: Viral titer measurements showed a trend toward lower ΔA51R titers in lungs at day 6, but this was not statistically significant (Figure 10E).

claim: By day 6 post-infection, VACV-WR titers in ovaries are significantly higher than ΔA51R titers.
source: By day 6 post-infection, however, we detected significantly higher virus titers (p<0.05) in the ovaries of all VACV-WR-infected animals compared to ΔA51R-infected animals, in which virus was detectable in only 1/5 animals
evidence: Viral titer measurements showed significantly higher titers (p<0.05) in ovaries of VACV-WR-infected mice compared to ΔA51R-infected mice at day 6 (Figure 10F).

claim: ΔA51R cultures shed approximately twofold higher levels of EEV than VACV-WR cultures.
source: Our analysis revealed that, despite ∼10-fold lower titers of total (intracellular and extracellular) virus in ΔA51R cultures than in VACV-WR or ΔA51RFA51R cultures, ΔA51R cultures shed ∼twofold higher levels of EEV than VACV-WR or ΔA51RFA51R cultures
evidence: EEV measurements showed that ΔA51R cultures shed ~2-fold higher levels of EEV than VACV-WR cultures (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).

claim: IFN pre-treatment reduces VACV-WR and ΔA51RFA51R titers by approximately 10-fold by 24 hours post-infection.
source: Comparing the titers of VACV-WR, ΔA51R, or ΔA51RFA51R cultures pre-treated with IFN to parallel cultures without IFN treatment, we found that IFN pre-treatment reduced VACV-WR and ΔA51RFA51R titers by ∼10-fold by 24 hpi relative to control treatment.
evidence: Viral titer measurements showed that IFN pre-treatment reduced VACV-WR and ΔA51RFA51R titers by ~10-fold (Figure 10—figure supplement 1D).

claim: IFN pre-treatment reduces ΔA51R titers by approximately 10-fold by 24 hours post-infection, similar to VACV-WR.
source: ΔA51R titers, however, were similarly reduced at this time point, suggesting that loss of A51R does not make VACV more susceptible to the antiviral effects of IFN
evidence: Viral titer measurements showed that IFN pre-treatment reduced ΔA51R titers by ~10-fold, similar to VACV-WR (Figure 10—figure supplement 1D).
